articles.title: Comprehensive study of Algerian nettles: Phenolic content and multifunctional activities ofand
articles.full_text:
1

INTRODUCTION

Numerous folk and traditional remedies that have been used for thousands of years are based on plants. Plants are still thought to be a rich source of medicinal substances for the treatment and prevention of diseases. According to the World Health Organization, traditional medicines represent the major source of health care for almost 80% of the world's population. An estimated 35 000 or more plant species are currently used for medical purposes.A large number of studies have been conducted to determine the scientific explanation for the effectiveness of plants used in traditional medicine. The result was the discovery of chemical compounds, known as secondary metabolites, which are divided into several classes, of which the most studied is the class of phenolic compounds that possess good antioxidant effectsand exert significant effects on cardiovascular diseases, cancers, and aging, as well as a large number of other pathologies.Nettle is widely distributed. It is one of the rare plants that can be recognized easily. Nettle has fallen somewhat into oblivion because of its irritating sting.

Nettle is classified as a phytoalimurgic vegetable. This comprises the wild edible species that were consumed in the past during food scarcity.The main varieties identified under thespecies areL.,L.,L.,L.,Poiret.,Boiss.,Req.,Guss.,Pursh., andForst.Although nettle possesses good medicinal properties, it is considered as a weed.

This plant, a very important part of the local floral heritage, possesses several important pharmacological properties such as antimicrobial, anti‐inflammatory, antioxidant, antiulcer, and analgesic activities.It is used to treat all kinds of internal or external bleeding; results have shown its effectiveness in stopping nosebleeds and other hemorrhages.The current study investigated the medicinal properties of this plant that grows widely in the Tiaret region. Therefore, we explored some biological activities of two understudied common nettle species,L. andL.

2

MATERIALS AND METHODS

2.1

Plant material

Samples of nettles (and) were collected from the region of Tiaret, located on the southwest of Algeria (Monts of Guezoul: 35°23′38″ N, 1°18′22′′ E). These samples were obtained in January 2023 and authenticated by Prof. Ait Hammou Mohamed, botanist at the Department of Ecology, Faculty of Nature and Life Sciences, University of Ibn Khaldoun‐Tiaret (Algeria). The nettle leaves were picked by hand to separate them from the stems, sorted, washed, and dried at room temperature. Dried leaves were then pulverized in an electric mill, screened at a size of 200 μm, and kept in a dark, dry location until analysis.

2.2

Extraction procedure

Phenolic content was extracted from nettle leaves using maceration using two solvents (distilled water forand 70% methanol for). The extraction conditions and techniques were carried out according to Bouhenni et al.: 10 g of each sample was combined with 100 mL of each solvent, and the mixtures were agitated for 24 h at room temperature. A rotary evaporator was used to evaporate all mixtures after they were filtered using Whatman paper No. 1. The dried extract was stored for further analysis at 4℃.

2.3

Phytochemical analysis

2.3.1

Determination of total phenolic content

Folin–Ciocalteu reagent was used to assess the total phenolic content in accordance with the method outlined by Maaroufi et al.; 2.5 mL of the reagent was mixed with 0.5 mL of each extract and 1 mL of 20% sodium carbonate. This mixture was incubated for 30 min in the dark at room temperature. A UV–Vis. spectrophotometer was used to measure the absorbance of solutions at 765 nm. The gallic acid calibration curve was used to determine the total phenolic content, which was represented as milligram gallic acid equivalent (GAE) per gram of fresh weight.

2.3.2

Determination of total flavonoid content

The total flavonoid compounds were estimated using the aluminum chloride method as reported by Djarmouni et al.After 1.5 mL of each extract was thoroughly mixed with 1.5 mL of aluminum chloride solution, the mixture was kept at room temperature in the dark for 30 min. The absorbance was measured using a UV–Vis. spectrophotometer at 415 nm. The findings were reported as milligrams of quercetin equivalent (QE) per gram of fresh weight.

2.3.3

Determination of condensed tannin content

According to Price and Van Scoyoc,condensed tannin analysis was performed by mixing 1 mL of each extract with 2.5 mL of a 4% methanol vanillin solution and 2.5 mL of HSO. The absorbance at 500 nm was measured after 15 min. The amount of condensed tannins was measured in milligrams of catechin equivalent (CE) per gram of fresh weight.

2.3.4

Determination of hydrolyzable tannin content

Mole and Waterman's approach was used to assess the number of hydrolyzable tannins; 3.5 mL of ferric chloride solution was mixed with 500 μL of extract. The absorbance was measured at 660 nm, 15 s after the addition of extract. Results were expressed as milligram of tannic acid equivalent (TAE) per gram of fresh weight.

2.3.5

Phytochemical screening

According to conventional procedures,phytochemical screening of plant extracts was carried out to determine the primary groups of chemicals (tannins, saponins, flavonoids, alkaloids, phenols, glycosides, steroids, and terpenoids) present in the extractsTable).

2.4

Chromatographic analysis (ultra‐high‐performance liquid chromatography diode array detection tandem mass spectrometry)

The extracts were subjected to qualitative analysis using ultra‐high‐performance liquid chromatography (UHPLC) using a Dionex Ultimate 3000 UHPLC+ system equipped with a diode array detector and an LCQ Fleet Ion Trap Mass Spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). A Hypersil Gold C18 column (50 × 2.1 mm, 1.9 μm) was placed at 25℃. In a gradient program with a flow rate of 0.250 mL/min, the mobile phase consisted of two solvents: methanol (B) and 0.1% v/v formic acid in water (A),,,,(Table). For data collection and UHPLC instrument control, Chromeleon, version 7.2, was used.

Methanol and LC–MS‐grade water were purchased from Fisher Scientific. HPLC‐grade formic acid was obtained from Carlo Erba (France).

Three detection wavelengths—300, 330, and 350 nm—were used to estimate diode array detector signals, which allowed for sufficient detection of the class of chemicals. A three‐dimensional ion trap with electrospray ionization (ESI) in negative ionization mode was used for mass spectrometric analysis. The following ESI‐source parameters were used: source voltage, 4.5 kV; capillary voltage, −41 V; tube lens voltage, −95 V; capillary temperature, 350℃; and nitrogen sheath and auxiliary gas flow, 32 and 8 arbitrary units. Mass spectra obtained by full‐range acquisition of/100–900 using a data‐dependent scan—the collision‐induced dissociation of identified molecular ion peaks ([M − H]) set at 30 eV—were used as an additional source of ionization. Data collection, analysis, and instrument control were performed using Xcalibur, version 2.1. Data processing and presentation were performed using Origin, version 7.5.

Retention durations, UV–Vis. spectra from the diode array detector, mass spectra with the associated molecular ion peaks, and distinctive ion fragmentation pattern of selected peaks (tandem mass spectrometry [MS/MS]) from corresponding UHPLC chromatograms were used to assign the identified compounds. Therefore, the detected compounds were identified by comparing the corresponding UV–Vis. and MS/MS fragmentation pattern, as well as the positions in the retention scale, with those found in the available literature and spectral databases (with high confidence level). For some compounds with the same molecular ion peak/values and similar spectral data, identification was limited to the class and different isomer, with lower confidence level. Compounds with no spectral matches in the available literature and spectral databases and reference standards used were treated as not identified. Detected compounds were also identified using reference standards, for some of them such as citric acid, 3‐‐caffeoyl‐quinic acid, 5‐‐caffeoyl‐quinic acid (5‐CQA), caffeic acid (Sigma), and apigenin (Extrasynthese, France), with the highest confidence level.

2.5

Biological activities

2.5.1

Antioxidant activity

According to Snighda and Thakur,the 2,2‐diphenyl‐1‐picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) free radical scavenging method was used to assess the antioxidant activity of nettle extracts. After 1 mL of methanolic DPPH solution (0.1 mmol/L) was mixed with 1 mL of nettle leaf extracts, the samples were left in the dark for 30 min. A spectrophotometer was used to detect absorbance at a wavelength of 517 nm.

The antioxidant activity was estimated using the following formula:whererepresents the absorbance of the DPPH solution without the extract and Asample is the absorbance of the DPPH solution with the sample. According to reports, the half‐maximum inhibitory concentration (IC) is the quantity of antioxidant needed to reduce the initial DPPH concentration by 50%.

2.5.2

Antibacterial activity

The disk diffusion method was used to assess the extracts' antibacterial effectiveness against five different bacterial strains:(ATCC 27853),(ATCC 19606),(ATCC 35659),(ATCC 6538), and(ATCC 14579).

Mueller–Hinton broth was used to inoculate bacterial strains for 24 h at 37℃. To achieve initial cell counts of ~10CFU/mL, the suspensions were standardized using a UV–Vis. spectrophotometer; 10 μL of each extract (10 mg/mL) was impregnated onto sterile disks with a diameter of 6 mm. Standard antibiotics were used as positive controls. Antibacterial activity was calculated by measuring the diameter of the clean zone surrounding the disc and expressing the result in millimeters.

2.5.3

In vitro antihemolytic activity

The spectrophotometric approach was used to measure the antihemolytic activity; 5 mL of fresh whole blood was drawn from a healthy and nonsmoking volunteer (Prof. Koula Doukani, coauthor), who did not take any medicines or alcoholic beverages for at least 2 weeks, and centrifuged for 10 min at 3000 rpm. Sterile phosphate buffer saline solution (pH 7.2) was used to wash the blood pellet thrice. A standard 0.5% saline solution was used to resuspend the pellet.

The extracts' ability to prevent hemolysis caused by HOwas assessed using the method of Nabavi et al.; 2 mL of erythrocyte suspension (4%) and 1 mL of each extract at varying concentrations (100–500 μg/mL) were mixed, and the reaction mixture's volume was increased to 5 mL using phosphate buffered saline. The reaction mixtures were incubated at 25℃ for 5 min, and then 0.5 mL of HOsolution was added. The reaction mixtures were centrifuged at 2500for 10 min after incubation at 25℃. The reaction mixture's absorbance was measured at 540 nm. To achieve 100% hemolysis (negative control), 2 mL of HOwas mixed with 2 mL of red blood cell suspension. 2.5.4

Microscopic observation of the smear

In accordance with El Bekkali,the May–Grünwald–Giemsa technique was used to stain the fixed blood smears for 5 min in May–Grünwald stain diluted with an equal volume of distilled water. Then, without washing, the smears were placed in Giemsa stain diluted with 9 volumes of distilled water for 30 min. Finally, the smears were washed with distilled water and allowed to dry; then the stained blood cells were examined under a light microscope.

2.5.5

Statistical analysis

The data obtained in this study were analyzed using one‐way analysis of variance (ANOVA). The statistical software SPSS, version 20, was used to generate all the results for this study;< 0.05 were considered statistically significant. The experiments were repeated a minimum of five times. The results were reported for each variable as mean ± standard error.

3

RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

3.1

Phytochemical analysis

3.1.1

Total phenolic content

To quantify the phytochemical components of nettle, phytochemical analysis was performed on nettle extracts ofand.

The results of total phenolic content of nettle species are shown in Figure.

The phenolic content ofobtained using maceration with methanol (70%) was 25.27 ± 0.29 mg GAE/g of fresh weight. However, phenolic content ofobtained using maceration with distilled water was 19.20 ± 1.25 mg GAE/g of fresh weight. Statistically, the results were significantly different between the two extracts (< 0.05).yielded better content compared to.

Daoudi et al.found that the methanolic extract ofcontained the highest phenolic content (2.313 ± 0.3 mg GAE/30 g DW) compared to(1.498 ± 0.09 mg GAE/30 g DW) and(0.06 ± 0.029 mg GAE/30 g DW), which confirms the current results. Also, Özen et al.studied the phytochemical profile of, which was lower than that found in our study (85.40 ± 7.77 μg GAE/g of fresh weight).

Several studies on the phenolic content of aqueous extract offrom many countries produced similar results, with a concentration of 12.5 ± 0.53 mg GAE/g of fresh weight for Algerian nettle,14.41 ± 0.80 mg GAE/g of fresh weight for Lybian nettle,29.56 mg GAE/g DW for Tunisian nettle,and 109.768 ± 3.60 μg GAE/mg DW for Moroccan nettle.

The current results were much higher than that found by Kataki et al.,which is 6.36 mg GAE/g of fresh weight forobtained in October.

Also, Pourmorad et al.reported values close to our results: 24.1 mg GAE/g of fresh weight for the methanolic extract (50%) of. However, our values remain lower than those found by Zemmouri et al.: 85.11 ± 0.5 mg GAE/g of fresh weight for the ethanolic extract ofand 30.79 ± 0.96 mg GAE/g of fresh weight for the aqueous extract.

The results differ from literature due to geographical, seasonal, environmental, harvesting, genetic diversity, plant parts, extraction protocol, solvent, and storage conditions. Differences in phenolic compound results can be attributed to varying solvents and storage conditions.,

Also, the solubility of phenolic contents depends on the type of solvent used; for a high yield of polyphenols, methanol is the appropriate solvent.,However, Nencu et al.and Srivastava et al.found that the phenolic content is attributed to the plant's maturation phases (season: plants generally mature in spring); this could explain the low phenolic content found inandin the present study, as the plant was harvested in mid‐winter.

3.1.2

Total flavonoid content

The flavonoid content of nettle extracts is shown in Figure.

The flavonoid content ofmethanolic extract is 15.4 ± 0.8 mg QE/g of fresh weight, whereas that ofaqueous extract was 18.3 ± 0.28 mg QE/g of fresh weight (Figure). The statistical test showed the presence of significant difference between extracts (< 0.05).

Our results are significantly higher than those obtained by Belhaddadfor petroleum ether extract of(1.96 ± 0.1 mg QE/g of fresh weight).

Previous studies on the aqueous extract ofhave reported varying amounts of flavonoids. They found the flavonoid content to be 11.9 ± 0.5 mg QE/g of fresh weight for Algerian nettle,2.57 ± 0.23 mg QE/g of fresh weight for Lybian nettle,5.34 mg QE/g DW for Tunisian nettle,and 10.98 ± 0.39 μg QE/mg DW for Moroccan nettle; these results were in the range of the present study.

Moreover, Toubal et al.recorded that the aqueous extract of great nettle () was rich in flavonoids: 150.30 ± 0.06 mg QE/g of fresh weight.

According to Bruneton,this discrepancy can be accounted by the fact that the harvest period, the area, and the extraction technique vary. A second parameter that could be responsible for the difference in flavonoid content is their solubility. The solubilization of flavonoids depends on their glycosylation; heterosides are soluble in water and alcohol or the mixture, whereas others possess extremely low water‐soluble properties. Lipophilic flavonoids such as aglycones are directly extracted using nonpolar solvents.

However, Maaroufi et al.revealed that the most polar solvent (water) had the lowest extraction capacity for all the flavonoids examined, suggesting that the solvent's polarity does not appear to affect extraction. Flavonoids are polyphenolic pigments that contribute, among other things, to the coloration of flowers and fruits. They perform a significant number of functions and possess numerous antioxidant properties; they are particularly active in maintaining good circulation.

Some flavonoids also possess anti‐inflammatory, antibacterial, and antiviral properties.These compounds are largely influenced by genetic factors, environmental conditions, the degree of ripeness, and their storage conditions; they are ubiquitous compounds in the plant kingdom.

3.1.3

Condensed tannin content

The condensed tannin content ofmethanolic extract andaqueous extract is shown in Figure.

The highest content of condensed tannins was observed in the aqueous extract of, 27.76 ± 1.80 (mg CE/g of extract), compared to the methanolic extract of, which was 3.46 ± 0.27 (mg CE/g of extract). From a statistical standpoint, a significant difference was observed betweenandextracts (< 0.05).

A few studies determined the quantity of tannins in the aqueous extract of; the results were lower than those of our study: 8.5 ± 0.2 mg GAE/g of fresh weightand 4.05 mg GAE/g DW.

The results found by Zemmouri et al.were similar to our results, with 6.29 ± 1.03 mg CE/g of fresh weight (ethanolic extract) and 1.05 ± 0.34 mg CE/g of fresh weight (aqueous extract) of.

3.1.4

Hydrolyzable tannin content

The results of hydrolyzable tannin content of nettle extracts are shown in Figure.

The content of hydrolyzable tannin inaqueous extract was higher than that ofmethanolic extract, with values of 8.14 ± 0.19 and 2.5 ± 0.25 mg TAE/g of fresh weight, respectively (Figure). Statistical analysis demonstrates a significant difference between the two extracts (< 0.05).

Our results fall within the range cited by Nencu et al.,who investigated the effect of the stage of maturity by harvestingfrom March to July and using methanol for extraction (7.4 and 11.1 mg TAE/g of fresh weight).

The highest content of condensed tannins was obtained by Nencu et al.,which is (16.855 ± 1 mg TAE/g of fresh weight) for the methanolic extract ofharvested in May. These outcomes are significantly better than the current ones.

According to Altemimi et al.,tannins are polyphenols that share the common property of astringency by precipitating certain proteins in saliva. Tannins, derived from human consumption, have medicinal properties, including antiviral, antitumor, tissue regeneration, and skin toning, influenced by their structure and polymerization degree.

3.1.5

Phytochemical screening

The results of qualitative assay of samples are presented in Table.

The presence of alkaloids, flavonoids, tannins, and terpenoids and the absence of anthocyanins, reducing compounds, cardiac glycosides, and mucilages are confirmed in both species. The absence of saponins and the presence of sterols and polyterpenes are observed in, unlike in. Similar results confirm that the present findings have been observed by several authors who have worked on species of the same plant. Indeed, Safanah et al.in their study in Iraq reported high levels of tannins, flavonoids, saponins, and alkaloids in.

Studies conducted onin Turkeyand in Russiarevealed the presence of flavonoids and tannins. Also, Moses and Robertdescribed this plant as a rich source of saponosides, alkaloids, glucosides, and coumarins. Chaouche et al.revealed the presence of tannins, gallic and catechin tannins, flavonoids, anthocyanins, alkaloids, saponins, glucosides, and mucilages in nettle leaves (). The results of the phytochemical test conducted by Laoufishowed that the leaves of the great nettle harvested in Dellys (Algeria) contained total tannins, gallic tannins, flavonoids, saponosides, mucilages, and alkaloids.

Moreover, Belmamoun et al.observed a high concentration of phenolic compounds in the methanolic extract of, which was characterized by a more significant presence of saponins; a moderate level of tannins; a low concentration of flavonoids, free quinines, and sterols; and the absence of alkaloids.

3.1.6

Chromatographic analysis (‐‐/)

Results of chromatograms (from diode array and mass chromatographic detectors) are shown in Figures,,,forandextracts. Numerous compounds were identified in the extract samples (Table). Two main classes such as phenolic acid and other acids and their derivatives (compounds 5–9, 11–13, 17 and 2–4, 19) and flavonoids (compounds 10, 18, 20) were detected in the extracts, with high levels of 5‐CQA and 4‐‐caffeoyl‐quinic acid (4‐CQA) (compounds 7 and 9, respectively; Table) in both extracts. Caffeic acid (compound 6) is the main constituent present only inextract. The corresponding UV–Vis. and MS/MS fragmentation pattern of some detected compounds are shown in Figures,,,,.

Absorption maximum for all compounds in the caffeoyl‐quinic, coumaroyl‐quinic, feruoyl‐quinic, and caffeic acid groups was between 300 and 330 nm in the UV–Vis. spectra, with the characteristic shoulder at a shorter wavelength (as shown in Figures,,,), which is in the accordance with the literature data.According to the elution order as well as fragmentation pattern in the mass spectra (MS/MS product ions), the 3‐, 4‐, and 5‐‐acyl derivatives of quinic acid have a characteristic spectral pattern, which is explained in Clifford et al.and Kuhnert et al.For example, base peaks at191 (100% of ion abundance) were followed by peaks at179, 173 161, 135 and 179 173 in the MS/MS fragmentation pattern, indicating 3‐and 5‐occupied positions in the quinic acid residue of the caffeoyl‐quinic acidsfor compounds 5 and 7 (Figure) and (Table) respectively; they were also identified with the highest confidence level by the corresponding reference standards. 4‐CQA was identified by the characteristic MS/MS fragmentation pattern (compound 9; Figure; Table), with a base peak detected at/173 followed by a peak at/179 and also peaks at/191 and/135.5‐‐Coumaroyl, 4‐‐coumaroyl, and 5‐‐feruloyl‐quinic acids (compounds 11, 12, and 13 in Table, respectively) were identified similarly using characteristic MS/MS fragmentation patterns.,The unsaturated fatty acids such as compounds 21–24 and one hydroxy‐coumarin (compound 1) were also detected in the extracts and identified by comparing with the corresponding spectral data found in the available spectral databases (Table). Three compounds had no spectral matches in the available literature and spectral databases and therefore not identified (compounds 14–16, Table). Compound 18 was tentatively identified as trihydroxy‐methoxyflavone‐rutinoside due to characteristic UV–Vis. spectrum (bands I and II in the ranges 240–280 and 300–380 nm, respectively) for the basic flavonoid structure and MS/MS fragmentation pattern in which molecular ion peak (/607) yielded a base fragment ion (/299) with the loss of rutinoside residue (308 units), as shown in Figureand Table.

Pinelli et al.reported that studies on the phenolic profile and HPLC analysis of cultivated and wild nettle () samples revealed that the cultivated leaf samples contained caffeic acid derivative,‐coumaric acid, chlorogenic acid, 2‐‐caffeoylmalic acid, rutin, quercetin 3‐‐glucoside, kaempferol 3‐‐rutinoside, and isorhamnetin 3‐‐rutinoside, whereas the wild leaf samples contained caffeic acid derivative,‐coumaric acid, chlorogenic acid, 2‐‐caffeoylmalic acid, rutin, quercetin 3‐‐glucoside, kaempferol 3‐‐rutinoside, and isorhamnetin 3‐‐rutinoside. They state that 2‐‐caffeoylmalic acid and chlorogenic acid constitute up to 76.5% of the total phenolic compounds. Other studies on the phenolic profile of nettle () grown in various parts of Turkey found that leaf samples from the Mediterranean region contained myricetin, quercetin, rutin, ellagic acid, caffeic acid, and chlorogenic acid but did not contain fumaric acid, gallic acid, and catechin. Researchers also found that leaves from the Agean region contained quercetin and‐coumaric acid but no fumaric acid, gallic acid, or catechin. Though there was a statistical difference between quercetin and fumaric acid, they observed that leaf samples from the Black Sea region did not contain gallic acid, fumaric acid, vanillic acid, catechin, caffeic acid, and chlorogenic acid. Finally, leaf samples from the Marmara region did not contain gallic acid, vanillic acid, isorhamnetin, catechin, caffeic acid, or chlorogenic acid; nonetheless, other standards were discovered.In another work, 41 polyphenolic compounds were found to be members of the following classes: flavonols, flavan‐3‐ols, flavones, isoflavones, flavanones, coumarins, benzoic acid, cinnamic acid, and other phenolic acids.Ozcan and Yamanused HPLC–MS to analyze a variety of plant species. Among these plants was nettle (), which contained 18 ppm of quercetin, 13 ppm of myricetin, and 7.2 ppm of kaempferol.

Of all the acids determined using the LC–MS/MS technique, the highest levels of 3‐‐caffeoyl‐quinic acid, succinic acid, and quinic acid were found in the leaves of wild Polish stinging nettle.Ðurovi'c et al.reported thatwas rich in 5‐CQA followed by rutin, caffeic acid, quercetin‐3‐‐galactoside, aesculin,‐hydroxybenzoic acid,‐coumaric acid, protocatechuic acid, vanillic acid, ferulic acid, and‐hydroxyphenylacetic acid.

Furthermore, Grauso et al.revealed the presence of caffeic acid, ferulic acid, sinapic acid and esculetin, caffeoyl malic acid, and‐5‐caffeoylquinic acid in the leaves ofextracts. Several studies show that the most abundant compound in nettle leaves is 5‐CQA.,,

Its antioxidant properties are due to its phenolic core conjugated with‐alkane chain, and it may reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes.Research on 5‐CQA and its isomers reveals its antibacterial, antioxidant, and cytotoxic properties, as well as its potent antioxidant properties in plant extracts.,A previous study has pointed out that 5‐CQA can be metabolically activated by cytochrome P450 (P450) enzymes, horse‐radish peroxidase/HO, and tyrosinase/Oto form a cytotoxic quinone intermediate.

Antioxidant activity

The antioxidant activity of nettle extracts was determined using the DPPH radical scavenging method; results are shown in Figure.

The highest percentages of inhibition were observed inandat a concentration of 500 μg/mL (82.76 ± 1.03% and 59.06 ± 0.94%) respectively. Statistically, there is a significant difference between extracts (< 0.05).

Tablepresents the inhibitory concentrations (50%) of quercetin and the methanolic and aqueous extracts of nettles.

The study found that the methanolic extract ofhas a potent antioxidant effect, similar to the findings of Özen et al.(427.7 μg/mL). Another work studied the potential activity ofusing the DPPH free radical scavenging method; the results showed that methanolic extract exhibited potent antioxidant activity with an ICvalue of 125.23 ± 0.83 μg/mL.Some authors studied the antioxidant activity of an aqueous extract of, and the ICvalue was found to be significantly different: 151.2 mg/mL for Algerian nettle,0.64 ± 0.8 mg/mL for Lybian nettle,142.94 ± 10.54 μg/mL for Tunisian nettle,and 335.1 ± 2.18 μg/ mL for Moroccan nettle.Kataki et al.'swork onfound an ICvalue lower than that of our study (102 μg/mL). Zemmouri et al.recorded ICvalues of 95.21 ± 1.71 and 152.34 ± 0.37 μL/mL for the ethanolic and aqueous extracts of, respectively, which are higher than those obtained for.exhibited a low antioxidant activity (423 μg/mL) compared to.

The ICvalue found by Dall'Acqua et al.,which is 419 ± 10 μg/mL, falls within the range of results for our two species. Dasmeet et al.concluded that methanolic extract yielded better results because it could better inhibit oxygen radicals compared to the aqueous extract. Another study conducted in Iran on two other nettle extracts at different maturation periods showed that the plant has a stronger free radical scavenging ability during flowering than after flowering, with an ICvalue of 8.4 ± 0.1 μg/mL for the aqueous extract during flowering and 11.7 ± 0.2 μg/mL after flowering, and 12.4 ± 0.1 μg/mL for the ether extract during flowering and 22.5 ± 0.2 μg/mL after flowering.Similarly, the study conducted by Güleron two types of extracts ofcultivated in Turkey revealed an ICvalue of 300 μg/mL for the aqueous extract. According to Monfared et al.,the difference in efficacy ofmainly depends on the collection region and the physiological stage of the plant. The study of Joshi et al.on the effectiveness of various extracts offrom India revealed the activity of the ethyl acetate extract against the DPPH radical, recording an ICvalue of 78.99 ± 0.171 μg/mL compared to the other extracts, which had ICvalues of 168.2 ± 0.364, 215.96 ± 0.066, and 302.90 ± 0.141 μg/mL, respectively, for‐butanol, petroleum ether, and finally the ethanolic extracts, indicating the effect of the extraction solvent on the inhibitory efficacy of the extract.

The strong correlation between the total polyphenol concentration and antioxidant activity of the nettle extracts suggests that phenolic compounds likely contribute to this antioxidant capacity, according to multiple study groups.,Commonly referred to as chlorogenic acid, 4‐CQA and 5‐CQA possess antioxidant activity mainly via scavenging free radicals and preventing lipid peroxidation. By donating electrons or hydrogen atoms to counteract dangerous free radicals, they prevent cellular damage and function as antioxidants.Phenolic hydroxyl groups in 4‐CQA and 5‐CQA enhance their antioxidant properties by neutralizing free radicals like reactive oxygen species and hydrogen atoms.Research suggests that 5‐CQA may be a stronger antioxidant due to its hydroxyl group arrangement and stable‐semiquinone formation. CQAs, particularly di‐caffeoylquinic acids, can chelate metal ions like Fe, which can stimulate the production of dangerous free radicals, preventing oxidative damage by attaching to them.Caffeoylquinic acids can scavenge nitrogen‐centered radicals DPPH, ABTS (2,2'‐azino‐bis‐(3‐ethylbenzothiazoline‐6‐sulfonic acid)) and PTIO (2‐phenyl‐4,4,5,5‐tetramethylimidazoline‐1‐oxyl3‐oxide), suggesting they may use a direct antioxidant method to reduce oxidative stress. They can protect bone marrow–derived mesenchymal stem cells from OH‐induced damage through mechanisms like electron transfer, Htransfer, and Fechelation. However, antioxidant levels vary among compounds due to the positions of caffeoyl moieties and cyclohexane skeleton.,Phenolic concentration in plants is significantly influenced by exogenous and endogenous factors, leading to significant differences between species, with genetic factors being a key criterion for variability.

3.2.3

In vitro antihemolytic activity

Erythrocytes, with high polyunsaturated fatty acid membranes and redox‐active hemoglobin molecules, are a primary target for free radicals. Hydrogen peroxide treatment breaks down cell membranes, releasing hemoglobin and mobilizing Feby Ca, leading to OH radicals and cell lysis. Antihemolytic activity is due to multiple antioxidant processes.

The results of antihemolytic activity as a function of the different concentrations used for quercetin and methanolic and aqueous extracts of nettle leaves of both species are shown in Figure.

The results show that there is a proportional relationship between the concentration of the sample extract and the antihemolytic activity. However, the highest inhibition percentages were recorded at a concentration of 500 μg/mL (76.26 ± 0.54% and 60.75 ± 0.98%) inand, respectively. Statistically, there is a significant difference between the two extracts (< 0.05).

Tablepresents the 50% inhibitory concentrations of quercetin, methanolic extract, and aqueous extract of nettles.

The present results show that the lowest ICvalue of 327 μg/mL was obtained from the methanolic extract of, exhibiting the best antihemolytic activity, whereasaqueous extract had an ICvalue of 412 μg/mL. The powerful effect of nettle extracts against hemolysis was demonstrated using the leaves of both extracts; the present results propose that plant extracts exhibit an effect similar to the standard (IC= 348 μg/mL).

3.2.4

Microscopic observation

In the second part of this study, the results of the previous step were confirmed by microscopic observation of both extracts in the presence of controls. Microscopic observation proved that our two extracts exhibit significant antihemolytic activity. The methanolic extract ofhas the most potent antihemolytic activity, which preserves the intact shape of the red blood cells (Figure).

The bioactive constituents of erythrocyte hemolysis inhibitory activity, attributed to their concentration‐dependent properties, protect biological macromolecules like lipids and membrane proteins from oxidative degradation.Nettle leaf extract has antihemolytic properties due to its flavonoid content, which preserves red blood cells from oxidation and reduces lipid peroxidation, strengthening their resistance to lysis.Hemolysis by hydrogen peroxide occurs at low concentrations due to oxidative damage to the cytoplasmic membrane, causing lipid peroxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids. High concentrations result in erythrocyte lysis due to aggregation and hemoglobin insolubility due to polymerization.,,The antihemolytic effect in extracts is due to secondary metabolites like flavonoids and polyphenols. Flavonoids have antiradical properties, neutralizing free radicals. Polyphenols slow down the Fenton reaction, chelating transition metals like Feand stopping hydroxyl radical‐induced oxidations.,,Phenolic compounds inhibit methemoglobin synthesis after trapping hydrogen peroxide and reducing hydroxyl radicals, preventing oxidative damage and hemolysis.

Phenolic compounds integrate into the external hydrophilic layer and do not affect the fluidity of the hydrophobic portion, according to Bonarska‐Kujawa et al..Therefore, the rate at which these compounds are incorporated into the hydrophilic portion of biological membranes determines their protective effect. The extract's phenolic components appear to serve as a barrier to protect the cell from externally aggressive chemicals like free radicals by integrating into the hydrophilic portion of the membrane.The antihemolytic effect of plant extracts can be attributed to the fact that the extract balances the osmotic pressure between the two environments, or binds to the aquaporin, which prevents water from entering the red blood cells.This study is the first to characterize and evaluate the antihemolytic activity of two Algerian nettle species, focusing on phytochemical analysis and antioxidant and antibacterial activities in the Tiaret region.

CONCLUSION

This study explores the potential of Algerian nettle (and) as a medicinal plant for treating diseases. The study found thatspp. have antioxidant, antibacterial, and antihemolytic properties, correlating with bioactive phytochemicals. These properties could be applied for preventive or therapeutic purposes in diseases and food processing applications. However, there is a significant gap in in vivo research and clinical trials utilizing plant‐based preparations or isolated phytochemicals fromspp.

Abstract

Background

This study investigated the phenolic profile, antioxidant capacity, antibacterial effect, and antihemolytic activity of nettle leaves from two understudied Algerian species,and.

Methods

andleaves extracts were prepared by maceration using methanol and distilled water respectively. Their phytochemical analysis (total phenolic content, flavonoids, hydrolysable and condensed tannins) was determined. The chemical profle of these extracts was performed using ultra‐high‐performance liquid chromatography diode array detection tandem mass spectrometry. Antioxidant activity (using the 2,2‐diphenyl‐1‐picrylhydrazyl free radical scavenging method), antibacterial activity (using disk diffusion method), and antihemolytic activity were carried out.

Results

Results reveal high levels of flavonoids, tannins, alkaloids, and terpenoids. Several classes of compounds were identified in the extracts. Phenolic acid and other acids and their derivatives and flavonoids were detected in the extracts, with 4‐caffeoyl‐quinic acid and‐‐caffeoyl‐quinic acid being the main constituents in both extracts. Caffeic acid was also the main constituent present only inextract. For antioxidant activity of the methanolic extract ofand the aqueous extract of, the percentage inhibition value (82.76% and 59.06%) and the half‐maximum inhibitory concentration (IC) value (302 and 423 μg/mL)respectively, were obtained. Antibacterial activity of nettle extracts (10 mg/mL) demonstrated the sensitivity of pathogenic strain susceptibilityThe strongest antibacterial effect on tested strains was found in the aqueous extract ofagainst(21 ± 0.41 mm) compared to the methanolic extract of(16 ± 0.40 mm). The antihemolytic activity in the methanolic and aqueous extracts was 76.26% and 60.67%, respectively. The methanolic extract exhibited exceptional antihemolytic effect, with an ICvalue of 327 μg/mL, whereas the aqueous extract had an ICvalue of 412 μg/mL.

Conclusions

The study confirms the presence of bioactive substances in the nettle species, including flavonoids and tannins, which possess antioxidant, antibacterial, and antihemolytic properties, and can be processed into food and pharmaceutical products.

This study investigates the phenolic profile, antioxidant capacity, antimicrobial effect, and antihemolytic activity of nettle leaves from Algerian speciesand. Results show high levels of flavonoids, tannins, alkaloids, and terpenoids in the extracts. The main classes include phenolic and other acids, with 4‐‐caffeoyl‐quinic acid and 5‐‐caffeoyl‐quinic acid being the main constituents. The extracts also exhibit antibacterial activity, with the strongest effect against.
